subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-RULING BY MR. SPEAKER ON ALLEGED IRREGULARITY IN TABLING OF DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
On Thursday last the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) rose on a question of privilege in relation to the tabling of a report by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier). When tabling the paper, the Secretary of State used the following words:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table a report concerning the security agents in some of our national museums, which report constitutes a reply to the numerous questions put to me in the house in the last few days.
The report appears to have been presented to the house under Standing Order 41(2). The hon. member for Peace River has expressed the view that the terms of the Standing Order are not sufficiently broad to include the tabling of that particular document. The hon. member has been supported in his contention by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has submitted the additional argument that the Secretary of State contravened the rules and practice of the house when he replied to oral questions by tabling the answer under the provisions of Standing Order 41(2). In reply to these objections, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) suggests that Standing Order 41(2) should be given a wide, rather than a restrictive, interpretation. The substance of the minister's argument is summed up in the following words reported at page 4928 of Hansard of Thursday, January 30:
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
While Standing Order 41	(1) is really quite
precise as to the documents referred to, Standing Order 41 (2) is in the broadest possible terms. It permits a minister or a parliamentary secretary to lay on the table of the house any report or
other paper dealing with a matter coming within the administrative responsibilities of the government. I believe that the Chair should give the widest interpretation to those words.
Later Thursday afternoon, after the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) had raised his question of privilege, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) tabled a notice of motion to amend the Income Tax Act and the Estate Tax Act pursuant to Standing Order 60, subsection (1).
Then, pursuant to Standing Order 41(2) he attempted to lay on the table a document which the minister described as "explaining the ways and means motion and giving some illustrations of the consequent changes in taxes".
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), supported in his views by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), took exception to the procedure. The Chair then suggested that no further proceedings be taken and that the tabling be held in abeyance while the point of order and the previous question of privilege were being considered.

It is fitting to consider first the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) about the tabling of a document by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) . The hon. member, as well as others who supported his question of privilege, contend that the said document is not one which can be tabled under standing order 41(2). Secondly, they argue that the minister erred when he attempted to reply to questions put by some hon. members by another method than that prescribed by the standing orders. After much thought, I must decide in favour of the hon. members who questioned the procedure used, and especially the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who raised the second objection.
According to the standing orders, a question put during the daily oral question period may be answered either by an oral answer, by an order for return or by a ministerial statement on motions. I must express the opinion that the new standing order 41(2) does not provide for the establishment of a new procedure or answering oral questions.

February 3. 1969
Tabling of Documents
Therefore I must conclude that the question of privilege was justified. I suggest to hon members that as far as answers to questions are concerned, standing order 41(2) should be given that interpretation.

I should like to consider now the procedural point raised in connection with the effort by the Minister of Finance to table the memorandum to which I have already alluded. As hon. members know, Standing Order 41(1) corresponds word for word with the previous rule, Standing Order 40, subsection (1). The Standing Order reads as follows:
Any return, report or other paper required to be laid before the House in accordance with any Act of Parliament or in pursuance of any resolution or Standing Order of this House may be deposited with the Clerk of the House on any sitting day, and such return, report or other paper shall be deemed for all purposes to have been presented to or laid before the House.
That rule, corresponding, as I have said, to the previous Standing Order 40(1) determines the class of documents or papers that must be tabled by a minister pursuant to a statutory provision or to a standing or other order of the house.
The house has now adopted another Standing Order, 41(2), which reads as follows:
A minister of the Crown, or a parliamentary secretary acting on behalf of a minister, may, in his place in the house, state that he proposes to lay upon the table of the house, any report or other paper dealing with a matter coming within the administrative responsibilities of the government and, thereupon, the same shall be deemed for all purposes to have been laid before the house.
The new Standing Order can be interpreted in only one of two ways; either it is intended to provide another method of tabling the papers described in Standing Order 41(1) or it is intended to provide a method to table documents other than those provided in 41(1). In my view, the second interpretation only is logical. Indeed, if Standing Order 41(2) means anything, it must be that it enlarges the class of papers which can be tabled by the government without notice and without leave.
The Chair is bound by the clear words of the rule to the effect that a minister may table any report or other paper dealing with a matter coming within the administrative responsibilities of the government. So long as the report or paper deals with a matter which comes within the administrative responsibility of the government, and that the paper is an official document for which the minister or parliamentary secretary accepts responsibility, it can be tabled pursuant to Standing Order 41(2).
If this interpretation of the rule results in the tabling of a type of paper or document which had not been contemplated by the procedure committee, it is of course open to the members of that committee to review the Standing Order and redraft it in a way which would justify a more restrictive interpretation. For the time being, the Chair would be inclined to accept, for tabling, papers or reports which deal with matters coming within administrative responsibility of the government and which are official papers in the sense that they are proposed to the house by a minister, either directly or through his parliamentary secretary, in the exercise of his ministerial responsibility.

1.	Does the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have a specific policy regarding the use and distribution of time it allots to (a) apolitical movements (b) political movements (c) others for public information over its networks, both (i) radio, and (ii) television?

February 3, 1969
Questions
2.	If so, when was the policy adopted and on what principle (s) is it based?
3.	If not, will such a policy be adopted and when?
4.	If there is no intention of adopting such a policy, for what reason?

I am informed by the C.B.C. as follows: 1. Yes. Free time is allocated to bona fide political parties for the expression of opinion. There is no allocation of free time to groups other than bona fide political parties but the Corporation applies to all controversial issues the principles enunciated in reply to Part 2.
2.	The policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation governing political and controversial broadcasting was adopted in the early years of public broadcasting and is based on the following principles: (i) The air belongs to the people who are entitled to hear the principal points of view on all questions of importance; (ii) The air must not fall under the control of any individuals or groups influential by reason of their wealth or special position; (iii) The right to answer is inherent in the doctrine of free speech; (iv) The full interchange of opinion is one of the principal safeguards of free institutions.
The C.B.C. does not sell time to individuals or commercial concerns for broadcasts of opinions or propaganda. It furthers the foregoing principles by the provision of free time to competent speakers to present, without let or hindrance, varying points of view on questions of the day. The C.B.C. considers that the best safeguard of freedom of discussion is a policy which permits fair opportunity for the expression of varied points of view on issues of public interest and concern.
C.B.C. policy with regard to party political broadcasting is based on the fact that for the proper functioning of representative and democratic government, it is essential that the public should be fully informed of the issues at stake in any provincial or federal election, and of the position and policies of the various parties on these issues. To carry out this policy, the C.B.C. follows a general plan for party political broadcasting which includes the provision of network time free of charge to recognized political parties during general elections. This gives all qualifying parties the opportunity of speaking to a wide public, irrespective of their capacity to buy time. In the periods between elections, an amount of free, network time is

made available to recognized party leaders or their representatives.
The allocation of free time broadcasts between elections traditionally has been established at a meeting between the C.B.C. and qualifying parties held at the beginning of each new Parliament.
Free time broadcast periods during election campaigns are also allocated in immediate consultation with the parties.

Is the Road and Motor Vehicle Traffic Safety Office giving consideration to testing "artificial gravel" a substance used in improving highway safety by grading dangerous curves?

As indicated in my announcement of October 17, 1967, outlining the responsibility of the Department of Transport in the field of motor vehicle and highway safety, the new office will have responsibility for program co-ordination and the establishment of safety standards. Therefore, the Road and Motor Vehicle Traffic Safety Office will not itself undertake tests on "artificial gravel" or similar road building materials.
The Road and Motor Vehicle Traffic Safety Office is closely following the progress of tests currently being made by a number of agencies, including some provincial government departments and particularly those relating to skid resistance of pavement surfaces to traffic accidents. The relationships between aggregate texture, polishing and skid resistance have not as yet been completely evaluated.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have already complied with this request. If the hon. gentleman would look at the agenda that we have tabled, he would see that the matter of distribution of powers has a high place on the agenda and that within distribution of powers we specify fiscal matters and the spending power of the federal government.
I think it is important for the public to understand that the constitutional aspects of the spending power are really the ones that should be discussed. When the provinces are worried about the federal government's interfering-as they say-in certain provincial priorities, what they are really doing is calling into question the spending power as exercised for 100 years by the federal government. We are prepared to reopen discussion on this if and when the provinces want, except that we do believe that it is essentially a constitutional matter. We also believe that the provincial demands for discussing this matter can fit very easily within the agenda, which has been modified since November, to answer this demand by certain provinces.

speechtext: The house proceeded to the consideration of Bill S-14, to amend the Aeronautics Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. Baldwin (for Mr. Nesbitt) moved:
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITION, REGULATIONS, ETC.-REPORT STAGE
speechtext:
That clause 10 be added as follows:
10. The said act is further amended by adding thereto the following section:
13A. Any regulation, order or direction made under this act shall be filed with and considered by the standing committee of the House of Commons on Transport and Communications within one year of coming into force."
He said: This amendment will be the precursor of a number of amendments of this nature which we in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition will have occasion to move in respect of legislative proposals such as that contained in the amendment to the Aeronautics Act. During this first parliament since the election of June 25, which began in September, we have passed a number of bills. An examination of these bills would indicate the extent to which this government is moving aggressively and with determination to take more and more rights from parliament by way of granting powers to the government, various tribunals and boards, to legislate, to enact enactments of a prohibitory nature and the penalties in this respect. During the

February 3, 1963
Aeronautics Act
course of this parliament we see this being done more and more. We intend to file a caveat that in our view the government has been going too far and too fast.
I shall not attempt to breach the rules, but in support of the hon. member's amendment and the valid reasons behind it I simply want to call the roll of the bills which have gone through this house, some of which have been passed by parliament and others being in various stages of the legislative machine, having been given second reading by the House of Commons. For example, the post office bill gave vast, new powers, and from an examination of the steps taken in the debate in the house indicated that the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) already had very considerable powers to change postal rates and make variations and alterations in the vested rights of people. Almost half of what is proposed in the act to control pesticides, Bill C-154, is contained within the four corners of the regulatory sections. As a matter of fact, it has three sections dealing with regulations.
Then there are the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Farm Credit Act, the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. All these acts passed by the house provided that interest rates could be raised at the uncontrolled discretion of the Governor in Council. The Animal Contagious Diseases Act gives tremendous power to the Governor in Council in the fixing of individual compensation for people covered by the legislation. The C.N.R. financing bill for the first time gives to the Governor in Council the right to authorize the C.N.R. or any other national transportation corporation to float loans and arrange for the issue of securities. The bill before the house in respect of the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act gives power to regulate the granting of licences to pharmaceutical manufacturers.
Let me make it quite plain that I am not quarrelling, nor would I be allowed to quarrel, with the issues and principles dealt with under these authorizations. But I am entitled to emphasize the fact that we are slowly, in some cases not too slowly, taking out of this house the legislative power which is our right and turning it over to the executive. It may well be that these matters are essential. It may well be that in certain cases this is a desirable course to take, though I am very doubtful about that. But surely it is about time the members of the House of Commons, the press and the public became aware of the

extent to which the bureaucracy, the establishment and the executive are filching from parliament, from this house, the very important rights which are ours and which should not be left to the uncontrolled discretion of government. I challenge the validity of such action, I challenge the right to do it, I challenge the soundness of a philosophy of this kind.
The official languages bill, for example, grants to the proposed commissioner of languages the most drastic and formidable powers with regard to holding hearings in or out of camera and enforcing the provisions of the act. The powers this official will be granted, if the legislation passes, are simply fantastic. We all know that under the Customs Tariff legislation many years ago this house gave away to a very considerable extent the traditional right to impose taxation. Under the freshwater fisheries bill we gave to the government the right to fix the interest rate. Another example of this erosion of the rights of members of parliament is the bill to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act with which we shall be dealing later.
With regard to the bill to amend the Aeronautics Act, we find, for example, that one clause proposed by the government, and which we seek to take care of by the amendment tabled by the hon. member for Oxford, would take from the Governor in Council and give to the Air Transport Commission the right to make regulations. The practice followed by the government in this respect follows precisely what was done against my objection and the objection of a great many members of this party at the time the transport act was passed.
At that time we gave the Canadian Transport Commission the right to enact regulations in a vast area and fix punitive penalties for the infringement of those regulations. As a matter of fact, we removed from parliament and gave to the Transport Commission almost exclusive jurisdiction in the very important field of transportation. Transportation is vitally important to this country and to members of the house. The very foundation of this nation was predicated upon transportation and communications system which would draw together the various parts of the country. By the National Transportation Act we gave away those powers to the commission. Now the government is asking us to do precisely the same thing with regard to a number of powers and rights which, quite improperly, we gave away earlier to the Governor in Council. Now the Governor in
February 3, 1969

Aeronautics Act
Council is saying: We do not want them; we are going to pass them on to an appointed body which will deal with these questions as it sees fit.
It is for this reason that we have proposed the amendment which will provide that all orders, regulations and decrees made under the provisions of the Aeronautics Act must be brought, within one year of the time they assume the force of law, before the standing committee which is charged by the rules of this house with dealing with matters of transportation. I point out to hon. members that we are not asking that these regulations, orders and decrees not become effective, or that the right to pass them be withheld in the sense that unless the house approves them they are invalid. We are simply saying that all orders and regulations should be filed with the appropriate committee and that committee must then consider them.
I have no doubt that 90 or 95 per cent of the decrees, orders and regulations will be of no particular interest to the committee. But we are asking that the committee have the right to take an interest if in the opinion of any member of this house or, in particular, of any member of the committee, there has been an attempt to encroach and trespass upon the rights of the individual. In that event this house must give effect to the rights of members who are here as protectors of the rights of the people of Canada.
It is in that sense that this amendment has been moved. I ask all hon. members to support it. It is a matter which affects hon. members who sit on the government side as well as those who sit on this side of the house. I ask hon. members: Are you prepared to give away, without any question, these rights to the establishment, to the bureaucracy? After all, governments come and governments go, but these people stay for ever. I am not challenging their bona fides or the fact that they may be good people, fully capable of discharging their responsibilities, but I suggest it is an unsound principle for an elective body such as this house aimlessly and carelessly to give away to the executive branch of government all the powers which are being asked for here and in other bills. If we do this we shall be further validating what the government has done in the past and will continue to ask the house to do in most of the legislative proposals with which we shall deal before the session is ended.

If they are content to sit back quietly and acquiesce in this discharge of their responsibilities and in handing them over to the government, they are the people who will have to answer for it later. It is in that sense this amendment is moved, and I would request the co-operation and the support of hon. members in giving effect to it.

What the hon. member is really proposing is that we write into the statute, for all time, what the house normally does by way of an amendment to the Standing Orders. As hon. members know, we have recently gone through that process. Contrary to what is sometimes suggested, it is not necessary for parliament to change the Standing Orders; rather it is for the House of Commons to change its own Standing Orders.

As a result of the changes that were made recently to our Standing Orders, under Standing Order 65 the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications has been created. In view of the fact that the committee on procedure and organization is presently considering Standing Order 65 it is possible-certainly it is beyond mere quibble -that they may well wish to change the Standing Order again, perhaps to change the designation of this particular committee or to change its powers. Therefore, if we were to accept the hon. member's amendment we would need not only a decision of the house to amend the Standing Orders but would also have to bring in an amendment to the Aeronautics Act itself, which I suggest is really an absurd situation.
The hon. member for Edmonton West made reference to what was formerly Bill C-146 and is now the anti-dumping act in connection with the tabling in Parliament of certain papers to enable the house to dispose of them as it may wish. My second reason for not accepting an amendment of this kind at this time can be deduced from the remarks made by the hon. member for Peace River. Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That clause 1 be amended as follows:
Firstly, that proposed section lA(b) be deleted and the following substituted:
lA(b) "navigable water" includes a canal and any other body of water not wholly situated within a province and not directly connected to a further canal or body of water situated in another province, created or altered as a result of the construction of any work.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Secondly, that proposed Section 2(c)i be amended by adding thereto after the word "thereto" the following:
"constructed on a navigable water."
Thirdly, that proposed Section 2(c)iv be amended by adding after the word "navigation" the following:
"on a navigable water."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the reasons for moving these amendments to proposed sections 1A and 2(c) are twofold. They are for the purpose of clarifying a situation which has existed for a long time; in short, they are to clarify the term "navigable water". They are also introduced to try to prevent an attempted power grab on the part of the federal government of pieces of real estate that were never intended to come under the jurisdiction 
of the federal government. I am referring to farm ponds and the like. We were told in the committee that studied this bill that things like ponds would come within the purview of this legislation.
The term "navigable water" seems an express definition; yet the fact is that navigable waters are vaguely defined in the act, to say the least. To appreciate what I mean one must look at the British North America Act. Section 91, subsection 10, sets out that navigation and shipping come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government. Subsection 13 refers to "ferries between a province and any British or foreign country or between two provinces." Subsection 9 refers to "beacons, buoys, lighthouses, and Sable Island." Yet another subsection refers to waters. It is clear, therefore, that section 91 of the act does not clearly or precisely define the term "navigable waters". If the fathers of confederation had considered all waters navigable waters they would not have included specifically the words "ferries between a province and any British or foreign country or between two provinces". Neither would they have included subsection 9 which refers to "beacons, buoys, lighthouses, and Sable Island." It is clear, therefore, that the term "navigable water" was in some way limited in meaning.
It is also necessary to see what the fathers of confederation intended to say when the act was drawn up. At the time of confederation navigable waters were of greater importance to transportation in Canada than they are today. I doubt that in their wisdom the fathers of confederation, gray beards and all, could have seen into the future in the manner described in Lord Tennyson's poem "Locksley Hall" and foretold the great dams that would hold back water in populous parts of Canada. These structures have created large bodies of water and serve purposes of conservation. Conserving water and other resources was not a problem in 1867. Clearly, the fathers of confederation never envisaged that farm ponds, for instance, would come under the purview of the legislation. One must remember that when looking at the British North America Act.
There is also this question: what is navigable water? There have been a number of court decisions on the subject, but I shall not refer to them. Anyone can look up court records. To say the least, existing court decisions on the point are not decisive nor helpful.
February 3, 1969

When officials of the Department of Transport were before the committee and giving evidence they were as helpful as they could be but seemed unclear as to how to define navigable waters. Most of us agree, I think, that there is a difference between a body of water that is navigable and one that is not. For example, at one time the Thames River flowing through the city of London, Ontario, was navigable. Ships used it in 1890. At one time a steamer upset on the river and 90 people were drowned. Clearly, when that happened the Thames River must have been navigable. Now the river dries up in the summer months. Another example of a body of water that may be navigable at one time and not navigable at another is a body of water containing rapids. If the rapids can be eliminated logs can be floated down the river. The officials of the department define navigable water as any body of water on which you can float a raft, canoe, or anything else. While that may be a reasonable definition I do not think that the term "navigable" was ever intended to apply to waters on which you can float only a raft or canoe. The fact of the matter is that officials of the department themselves are not too sure of the effect of the amendments proposed by the minister.

This is correct, yes. I think the federal government has this as a result of the British North America Act where it has the authority for all matters relating to navigation on all bodies of water in Canada.
I do not want to spend time reading into the record of this house, but on other occasions it was pointed out this would include such bodies of water as farm ponds. I mentioned earlier that it was never intended by the British North America Act to give jurisdiction to the federal government over bodies

Navigable Waters Protection Act of water which were wholly within a province or unconnected with other bodies of water. No matter how one may interpret the terms of the B.N.A. Act, I think it becomes manifestly foolish to suggest it was ever in the minds of the fathers of confederation to include farm ponds and the like under the federal Department of Transport.
On the other hand, it is quite clear there must have been some doubts as to how far the federal government should proceed in this regard because of section 91 of the act and the various subsections to which I referred earlier. Navigable waters such as the Great Lakes, which are international, and the Saskatchewan River and the Ottawa River connecting two major provinces, would have to come under federal jurisdiction. But certainly it was never intended that every tiny creek or stream wholly within a province should come under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
The word "navigable" has been defined in statutes although in some fields there have been disputes from time to time. A river could be navigable at one time in history but not at another because it might dry up. The question is: when is a body of water navigable and when is it not? According to the officials of the Department of Transport it is any body of water, no matter how small, on which anything can float. This covers everything. This is very simple from the viewpoint of the officials of the department.
The general public would be startled to find out they need permission from the Department of Transport in order to build a dock in front of a cottage on a lake such as Lake Scugog, Rice Lake or the Muskoka lakes which are in no way connected with other lakes or provinces. The minister says: we think things will remain the same. Why then Mr. Speaker, are these powers being sought?
I do not understand. The officials of the department were not helpful in explaining these matters. They were very uncertain about the effect of the legislation. This legislation at first appeared to be housekeeping legislation. The drafting of the legislation appears to have been hasty, vague and sloppy, with great powers being conferred on the federal government which I do not think were intended.
I suggest that the reasons for the amendment are obvious. The bill seeks to include all small bodies of water, even farm ponds, which were never intended to come within


the ambit of federal powers. The amendment is carefully worded and reads:
"navigable water" includes a canal and any other body of water, not wholly situated within a province and not directly connected to a further canal or body of water situated in another province-
This is understandable and necessary for waterways such as the Rideau Canal system which, although wholly in the province of Ontario, clearly connects two bodies of water, one being the Ottawa River which divides two provinces and comes under federal jurisdiction. The Trent Canal connects two of the Great Lakes which are international bodies of water. In order to include these projects there would have to be reference made to connecting bodies of water although not directly connected. The reason for the amendment is obvious in the case of waterways such as the Thames, the Grand and various others where the waters have been dammed up to create conservation ponds or lakes, as they are called, and there is no way of moving out of these ponds by any vessel as defined by the act. There is no system of locks to get in and out of the lakes.
The amendment is related to section 92, subsection 10(c), of the British North America Act which states:
(c) Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the Parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
This refers to works such as dams and other construction.
When the fathers of confederation were framing section 92 of the act which gives rights to the provinces they realized that the definition of "works" might cause some trouble. The minister could perhaps clear up the question of what is navigable water and what is not by drawing up an amendment to the Navigable Waters Protection Act stating that for the purpose of this act certain waters will be deemed to be navigable, such as the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence, Ottawa, Saskatchewan and Niagara Rivers. From time to time certain waters used for navigation purposes could be so designated by order in council. This might be a better way of doing it. I do not know. At the present time I cannot imagine why officials of the Department of Transport would want to seek jurisdiction over every little body of water and puddle in the country. I am surprised at this sort of thing finding its way into a statute.

I have been in this house long enough to know that often it is difficult for a government to accept amendments proposed from the other side. There is always the question of losing face even if proposed amendments make sense, but I hope the minister will accept this amendment because it would relieve his department of a great deal of responsiblity.
If a man builds a dock on a small lake and his neighbour does not like it, under the terms of this bill the neighbour can run to the Department of Transport to raise cain about the dock. One would need to be on good terms with the local D.O.T. officials if one wanted to build a dock.
I think the minister should be happy to be rid of the responsibility for a lot of little rivers. If his department felt it was necessary to bring certain bodies of water under the act he could do it by order in council, and in this instance I think that would be the best way. My amendment would relieve the minister and his department of the responsibility for farm ponds and little creeks and at the same time would in no way interfere with what really are the waters that must concern him and his department, namely, large bodies of water on which ships travel between countries, including all of the St. Lawrence Seaway and a number of big rivers in western Canada and elsewhere.
I assume the minister will not be prepared to accept my amendment but I submit he should introduce some amendment to clarify

Navigable Waters Protection Act what is navigable water and what is not. His proposed amendments will create nothing but an administrative nightmare so far as many areas of Canada are concerned.
Giving the department responsibility over little bodies of water such as farm ponds and small inland lakes is simply to encourage spiteful actions between neighbours. If I do not like a dock that my neighbour is building, if I think he is building it out too far, I can go to the Department of Transport and complain. Nobody is suggesting that the minister should not have control over docks, floating platforms and other works on major arterial waters such as the St. Lawrence. My purpose in proposing this amendment is not based on pride of authorship. It is to clear up an administrative mess. The officials of the department have told us that the proposed changes in the act will cover tiny bodies of water and docks. They said major, important docks, but they were not sure what that meant. Certainly the minister indicated some surprise that the proposed changes would cover small, local docks and floating platforms. My objective is to try to keep a great many of us, including the minister, out of administrative arguments between local authorities and the department.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), I should like 
to thank all the members who sat on the committee on justice and legal affairs.
The minister has already had the opportunity of speaking to the House on the effects of the amendments proposed in this bill. The five proposed clauses were studied in detail by the committee on justice and legal affairs, where the minister himself dealt with each one of them.
It will have been noted that the unanimous report of the committee does not propose any change and I do not feel I need insist any further. Still, I shall review briefly the objectives of those five amendments.
The first is designed to facilitate the hearing of expert witnesses during trials; the second provides for more flexible cross-examination of the witnesses of one party; the third extends the definition of the word "Bank" to financial institutions; the fourth revises the rules on hearsay; finally, the fifth provides an honest solution to those problems which formerly arose from the form recognized for receiving oaths or solemn declarations.
In short, it modernizes the act with a view to promoting the achievement of a more just society.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in reference to clause 2 of the bill. The explanatory note reads as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to allow a party with leave of the court to cross-examine his own witness on a prior inconsistent statement made by him in writing, in order to enable the court to determine whether the witness is adverse.
I am a little concerned that the clause goes farther than the explanatory note, because it says:
Where the party producing a witness alleges that the witness made at other times a statement in writing-
It does not have to be proved. This point has come to mind recently, although I did mention it in the discussion on second reading. The provision means that if Crown counsel merely alleges that at another time John Brown made a different statement, he can have his own witness declared hostile and can cross-examine him. It is all right to bring the Canada Evidence Act up to date, but this question requires very careful consideration. The Crown may be having difficulty in proving some narcotics cases, and the Department of Justice may have merely handed this
February 3, 1969

provision to the minister without giving any-thought to it. If they did give any thought to it, they overlooked a problem that will arise.
When a person is charged with an indictable offence he is entitled to elect by whom he shall be tried. If he elects trial before a magistrate, the magistrate has jurisdiction to deal with the matter. The consent of the accused is required in this case. The accused may elect to have a preliminary hearing before a magistrate and trial in a high court before a judge and jury or a judge without a jury. In order to present at the trial the best possible case for his client, defence counsel cross-examines fully at the preliminary hearing in order to find out what is the Crown's case.
I should like to refer to a murder trial in which I was engaged in order to illustrate the point I am about to make. The police had obtained from the accused, who was charged with the murder of his wife, a confession. They had taken nine and a half hours to obtain a confession of 11 pages. The confession was made up of questions and answers, questions put by the policeman and answers given orally by the accused. After nine and a half hours the accused signed a statement which was declared admissible by the magistrate and by the trial judge.

The point I am making as to the credibility of the statement is that I noticed on reading the statement that nowhere had the police officer asked the accused: "Did you kill your wife?" One would have thought that in getting a statement through questions and answers this would be one of the questions the policeman would put to the accused. In crossexamination counsel asked: "Does this statement contain all the questions and all the answers material to the murder charge, the questions that were asked by the police officer and the answers given by the accused?" The police officer said "yes".
Then a question was asked by the defence counsel which would never be asked at a trial but which had to be put, namely: "Why was that question not put?" It should have been asked during a cross-examination which filled 11 pages and must have represented some kind of confession. The policeman answered: "I overlooked something. I did ask the accused that question but I forgot to write it in the statement and I forgot I asked him that question". The next question at the preliminary hearing asked by defence counsel was: "How many times did you ask that question?" 29180-3211

The policeman replied: "Once". He was then asked: "What was the answer?" That question would never be put before a jury because if the answer was "Yes, I stabbed or killed my wife" counsel would have hung his own client. I am not going to go into the answer that was given, but the answer given by the police officer differed from the one given at the time of the inquest.
Then defence counsel waited until the trial by jury started and asked the same question to build up the same set of facts, protected from incriminating his own client by the fact that he had sworn copies of the questions. Defence counsel asked: "Is everything that you asked the accused and everything the accused said in that statement?" The police officer, who was under oath at the preliminary hearing and whose memory failed him again or he did not know which side of the fence he was on, said: "Yes". Then he was asked: "Why did you not ask the accused 'did you kill your wife'?", to which he answered: "I forgot I did". It is a funny thing to forget. Then he was asked how many times he put the question, to which he said: "Once". So there was one answer at the inquest, one answer at the preliminary hearing, and a new answer before the jury. Of course the jury were not going to believe the police officer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack McIntosh (Swift Current-Maple Creek) moved:
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF FORMER PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the immediate organization of a program of medical examination of all members of the Canadian Active Service Forces who were prisoners of war in World War II, who have not been medically examined within the past five years either by the active treatment services of the Department of Veterans Affairs or on its behalf or by the Canadian Pension Commission to ascertain the effects of privation, malnutrition, injury or ill treatment on such personnel even before complaint of illness, if any, so as to forestall the onslaught of many disabilities and to prevent much later suffering and expense.
He said: I might inform the house, Mr. Speaker, that I was prompted to put this motion on the order paper after consultation with many of my colleagues in the Conservative Party, particularly those in our veterans affairs caucus committee. I am aware there have been previous representations to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube) on this subject, not only by veterans organizations and individual Members of Parliament
February 3, 1969

who have had to deal with this type of problem through correspondence with many of their constituents.
One of the main reasons for putting this motion on the order paper arises from conversation with the former minister of veterans affairs, now the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who has had experience not only as a prisoner of war and pensioner but has some idea of what we are trying to do. I would like for a moment to refer to correspondence between the hon. member for Edmonton West and the present Minister of Veterans Affairs. I do not have to say much about the letter sent to the minister on July 9, 1968, by the hon. member for Edmonton West, but perhaps to lay groundwork for further discussion on this motion I will read portions of both letters. In part the hon. member for Edmonton West stated:
On a number of occasions in the past I have spoken in the House and privately to your predecessor, about the advisability of now calling in all prisoners of war, save the so-called Hong Kong group for whom this has been done on a separate program, for a thorough physical examination. Many of these men are presently pensioners and their medical histories have been established by the Canadian Pension Commission. The great majority, however, have not been near doctors of the commission or of the departmental treatment services. So many of them should, for their own good and for the benefit of both the commission and your own officers. Long term effects of varying periods of privation and hardship (different than that of men who fought long hard battle campaigns) are at work and the results must be assessed.
He goes on to say:
Much valuable time has been lost as it is approaching 25 years since release.
He is referring to the former prisoners of war:
The fact that I was one of them and now have a limited pension entitlement should not blur my objectivity. I have discussed this at length with a number of ex-P.O.W. who generally share my views.
The minister replied that they were going to consider this matter. He said in part:
As you know, the Hong Kong survey was conducted by the medical advisory branch of the Canadian Pension Commission. It is generally agreed that during the period of their internment the Hong Kong prisoners were subjected to slave labour, maltreatment and starvation, and suffered from diseases not commonly known in Canada. As a result, they now have disabilities, the extent of which were not fully realized until revealed by the review.
I would add at this time that the same conditions, although possibly to a lesser
Prisoners of War Medical Examinations degree, apply to many of our veterans who were prisoners of war in Europe. The minister goes on to say:
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
From time to time there have been suggestions made to the Pension Commission by veterans and their organizations that prisoners of war from the European theatre of war be surveyed in the same manner as were the Hong Kong veterans. While the European prisoners of war suffered great privations, the commission has been able to assess with a great degree of accuracy the resulting disabilities-
I doubt that, Mr. Speaker.
-and accordingly it has been felt that there is not the same need for a review along the lines carried out in the case of the Hong Kong group.
With that statement I disagree. The minister goes on to say:
-the suggestion contained in the resolution passed at the Dominion convention of the Royal Canadian Legion outlines a slightly different procedure than that so far advocated. Your request is that all prisoners of war, aside from the Hong Kong veterans, be now given thorough medical examinations. Since this would include non-pensioners as well as pensioners, it could best be done by our treatment services, and I will ask them to consider the suggestion with a view to ascertaining the extent of the problem.
I hope the minister has consulted the treatment services branch of his department and that the result will be favourable. I say this because in many cases we have had requests for assistance from some of these men who were prisoners of war and who have no documentation as to their disabilities. On their release many prisoners of war were very glad to get home quickly and as a result of their urgency were not properly documented by our medical services at the time of their discharge.
Many of these men after their release felt they could go back into the stream of life, to their former vocations or into some new trade, and make a living for themselves and their families. We have received many briefs pointing out that some of them were not able to do this because the disabilities they suffered while prisoners of war have since shown up. Now they have difficulty establishing that their condition is the result of disability suffered during service to their country.
The nation has a national obligation to all of these men whether we admit it or not. Most of them were volunteers at the time that their country needed them. They dropped whatever they were doing and volunteered for service. Regretfully, I say, possibly the medical examination given to some of these
5068	COMMONS DEBATES	February 3. 1969
Prisoners of War Medical Examinations men when they were attested was not what we would have liked it to be, and now we get reports from the Canadian Pension Commission, when applicants apply for pensions, that the disabilies from which they are now suffering are of pre-enlistment origin. I do not see how the commission can make such a decision with the lack of evidence before it, since the medical examination at the time the men were attested was very scanty and in many cases did not detect >any disability.
I would also remind hon. members that we who have the privilege of sitting in this house representing the people of Canada have an additional obligation to see to it that our veterans are not just remembered on Remembrance Day for their services to their country but that they receive a square deal 365 days every year. This does not apply solely to the veterans for whom this plea is made. It applies to the families of the veterans, to the families of enlisted men who were prisoners of war and who are now suffering disability as a result of service to their country. We have an obligation and a responsibility to do what we can to further the desire of our country to look after our veterans.
The branches within the department have two responsibilities. Granted, one is to watch the pursestrings to see that no one gets a pension to which he is not entitled. However, I would say there is not enough emphasis given to the benefit of the doubt clause, section 70, about which we have heard so much. The other responsibility is to see that the country's obligation to those who served in the armed services is carried out.
To bring this matter a little closer home to members of the house, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say I know of several veterans on the House of Commons protective staff who are suffering because of their service to their country. For example, just the other day one member of the protective staff had a severe stroke. He is a disabled veteran. In fact ever since leaving the armed services he has lived with one lung. He thought he could carry on. However, because of chance, and maybe because of the nature of his duties, he suffered a stroke. He has been in receipt of only a 20 per cent disability pension stemming from his service to his country. Now his wife and children are going to suffer the consequences if he passes on, as many people do after suffering such attacks.
There are also other people serving on the protective staff who have nervous disorders which may or may not be as a result of service to their country, but we have ample

proof in briefs from various veterans organizations, complete with medical reports, to show that we in Canada and authorities in other countries are not yet aware of the results of spending a long time as a prisoner of war. I would like to read portions from some of these briefs but they contain some almost unpronounceable medical terms.
I am sure many hon. members will agree that the requests for assistance they receive from veterans fall into three categories. In this instance I am referring to late applicants who up until now have not made application to their country for a pension, those who are having difficulty in establishing that their present illnesses are attributable to war wounds.
This is very difficult in the case of what we call a good soldier. Most men who have served in the armed services know that a good soldier very seldom went on sick parade. If he could possibly walk he did not go on sick parade. I am not trying to belittle those who did get pensions, those who had complete medical reports, and I am not saying it was very easy for them to get pensions. But many men, no matter how ill they were, did not report to the M.O. unless they were carried there and forced to go to hospital. These are the people who are now having difficulty in establishing their right to the pensions that the people of this country promised them if they ever needed them. The people I am talking about are very proud. I know most hon. members must have a number of letters on their files from such persons.
The second category of request deals with the conditions of service under which men served, and the third relates to P.O.W.'s.
All of us know that when men were P.O.W.'s, particularly in the European theatre and I assume the same applies to other theatres, no medical records were kept of their disabilities and other troubles during the time they were P.O.W.'s. With respect to the Dieppe veterans I understand this covered a period of three and a half years. At the moment I am not referring to the Hong Kong prisoners who were looked after, perhaps not as well as we would have liked but I think they are quite satisfied with the treatment given them by the country they served. But there are a great number who were prisoners of war in the European theatre and who should get the assistance that the country promised them.
I could refer to many articles on this subject that have appeared in the press. I have a
February 3, 1969

large file on them but I do not want to take up the time of the house quoting them because I am sure someone on the government side will want time to reply.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I see the chairman of the Committee on Veterans' Affairs in the house. He may have something to say about this, and I know there are some members on this side of the house who want to say a few words. Let me refer to some of these articles which I have mentioned.
The first is from the Sault Ste. Marie Star dated May 7, 1966. The heading of the article is "Reneging on High Promises". Let me just read the -concluding paragraph:
It is hard to believe that, even twenty odd years after that period when nothing was too good for "the boys", Canadians in general can be complacent about this sort of reneging when it is brought to their attention.
Another article is taken from the Oshawa Times dated January 13, 1966. Again, I will just read the last paragraph:
None in Canada would quibble on the fact those veterans who remain deserve a new pension deal. As the Charlottetown Guardian says, the surprising thing is that they have been made to wait so long for it.
There are many articles which support this desire of the people of Canada. If those members of this house who are interested in the reason this motion was originally placed on the order paper want more support, let me refer to a brief presented to the committee on veterans' affairs by the national Dieppe Prisoner of War Association. I do not intend to read the brief, but the opening part reads:
The Dieppe raid, one of the most scaring engagements of the second world war took place on August 9, 1942.
Of the 5,000 Canadian troops who set out for the coastal town in Normandy only 2,000, mostly men who did not land, came back.
Records show that 1,946 men, most of them seriously wounded, were taken prisoner. It is also recorded that 72 of these men died in captivity.
The period of imprisonment for those who survived was approximately three years.
In 1953 the federal government established a war claims commission and named Mr. Justice Thane A. Campbell as chief commissioner.
In his report, Mr. Justice Campbell found that general maltreatment did exist in prisoner of war camps in Europe where Canadian troops were imprisoned and that extraordinary brutal treatment had been proved in many cases. The finding of the war claims commission resulted in granting almost equal awards to both Hong Kong and Dieppe prisoners of war.

The effects of imprisonment have for some years been a matter of grave concern to those Dieppe prisoners of war who still survive, and it is their hope that the government will instruct the standing committee on veterans' affairs to conduct an inquiry into their plight which is in so many ways identical to that of the Hong Kong prisoners.
Among these similarities are the prevalence of peptic ulcers, lumbar spine disabilities, nervous disorders and other problems commonly attributed to avitaminosis.
I am sure members are aware that a number of the staff of this house are among those referred to in this brief, which then states:
The Standing Committee on Veterans' Affairs have for some time known that the circumstances of the Dieppe prisoners of war should be reviewed along the lines of what has been done in the case of the Hong Kong prisoners.
That brief contains a number of recommendations, and sets out certain war conditions under which these prisoners of war existed. There are medical reports which indicate the actual disorders we can now look for in these former prisoners of war. All of us who know certain individuals who were prisoners of war can see signs of these disorders.
In order that this country live up to its responsibilities, I suggest that the minister or the chairman of the Committee on Veterans Affairs give serious consideration to this motion. I am sure the country would not begrudge the cost of this proposal. I understand that the amount of money given to all disabled veterans does not amount to any more than hon. members vote each year to the C.B.C. Were it not for the type of people who were prisoners of war there might not have been a Canada today, and perhaps there would not have been a C.B.C. There are some who might suggest we should have lost the war when we take this fact into consideration.
I am not aware of the number of veterans who might be called in under this survey. Perhaps some veteran or another member could provide that information. In any event, I do not think the number could be very great. It is the responsibility of all of us who have been elected by the people of Canada to see that this obligation is fulfilled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) for bringing this matter to the attention of parliament, and for this excellent way of focusing attention on the needs, if needs exist, for the treatment of our prisoners of war. They certainly do merit special consideration.
February 3, 1969

Prisoners of War Medical Examinations
With reference to the Hong Kong prisoners of war referred to by the hon. member, the parliamentary Committee on Veterans Affairs recommended that this group receive special consideration. No group of Canadian prisoners of war have ever suffered from starvation, slave labour, general maltreatment, and diseases not commonly known in Canada as did the Hong Kong prisoners of war during the period of their internment. Some of the diseases and disabilities which the Hong Kong prisoners incurred were not fully understood until the review by Dr. Richardson was completed. In fact, this review revealed that these men suffered much more severe disabilities as a result of avitaminosis than previously assessed. Consequently, pension increases, in many cases quite substantial, were granted.
While it is true that prisoners held in the European theatre suffered many privations it has, nevertheless, been possible to assess with a great degree of accuracy the extent of the disabilities resulting from such privations. Furthermore, the study of the plight of the Hong Kong veterans has given the commission a much sounder basis from which to work in dealing with the assessment of disabilities incurred by all prisoners of war. Of course, it goes without saying that if conditions common among Hong Kong prisoners become manifest in other prisoners, the same consideration will be given. In the meantime, prisoners of war of whatever theatre are free to request re-examination at any time. If such an examination reveals that pensionable conditions have become worse then, of course, the pension would be increased.
Representations, on behalf of Canadians who were prisoners of war in Europe, and particularly those taken prisoner at Dieppe in August of 1942, have been under study intermittently for years. The evidence examined to date does not indicate residual disability comparable in kind or degree to that experienced by prisoners in Japanese hands. Tentative plans have been drafted for a more comprehensive study beginning with a review of the records and files of ex-European prisoners.
Dr. H. A. Richardson, the deputy chief medical advisor, has made a study in depth of the points raised in the brief alluded to by the hon. member. Those points have been very carefully considered by the medical advisory branch in recent years.
e (5:40 p.m.)
The evidence examined to date does not indicate residual disability in ex-European

prisoners of war comparable in kind or degree to that experienced by prisoners in Japanese hands. In other words, the prisoners in Japanese hands suffered privations which resulted in residual disabilities, such as avitaminosis, which are not apparent in any other group of ex-prisoners of war, and there is no evidence to establish that the European prisoners of war merit the type of survey which was conducted of the prisoners of war held by the Japanese. It is obvious that since these prisoners of war held by the Japanese obtained certain additional benefits as a result of the survey undertaken some years ago, the European prisoners of war are demanding the same type of survey in the hope that they will receive the same benefits. As Dr. Richardson points out, there is no evidence to indicate that they would be in any way entitled to the benefits granted the prisoners of war held by the Japanese or that such consideration is merited.
As everyone knows, prisoners of war have over the years been given special consideration by both the Canadian Pension Commission and the treatment services of the Department of Veterans Affairs. These ex-prisoners of war are still free to report for medical examination for any condition, at any time. At the moment, the medical advisory branch of the Canadian Pension Commission has drafted plans for a more comprehensive study of the files of all ex-European prisoners of war, and this will start with a review of a random sample of records.
Dr. Richardson has suggested that the possibility of having a survey conducted by persons not connected with the Canadian Pension Commission or the Department of Veterans Affairs might be considered. While the results of any such survey, with particular reference to pension payments and treatment, would have to be considered by both the treatment services and the medical advisory branch, such a study would nevertheless have the advantages of being undertaken by an independent group.
Our medical advisory branch has already concluded, from the information they have obtained to date, that the ex-European prisoners of war suffered no special disabilities other than those suffered by the regular serviceman who was exposed to normal combat conditions. Under the circumstances, it might be thought by this group that any report prepared by our own medical advisers might be prejudiced. In any case, such an independent survey would either support the opinion of our medical advisory branch or indicate that
February 3, 1969	COMMONS
it is not necessarily correct. Further action, if it is found to be necessary, will without question be taken.

Mr. Speaker,
the hon. member has placed a very important matter before the house and I congratulate him for so doing. We, in this party, wholeheartedly support the purpose and intent of his motion. Thinking back to my own war years and those following the war, I can recall how grateful the Canadian public seemed to be to those men and women who offered their services at a time when the country needed them most. I can also remember how full of goodwill and resolve were the Canadian public at that time to see that nothing but the best was done for those who returned, not so much because they deserved it in their own right but as recognition of what had been done.
We are really recognizing what our veterans did. It is like giving a medal to somebody. It is a form of recognition of those men and women who did not come back. This is one of the ways in which we can remember them. All of us can remember standing for two minutes of silence in the cold weather of Remembrance Day and thinking that if there was something we could do to honour the memory of those who did not return, we would do it. This is one such opportunity that I think the house should take to ensure that we honour the memory of those who did not return. We can do it by accepting this private member's motion.
I think it would establish a very important principle if, instead of waiting for a veteran to be so incapacitated that he had to come pleading to the Department of Veterans Affairs for assistance, we would help him before he had to crawl to us. I think this is important. If somebody comes pleading to you and you help him, it is not quite the same thing; you are in effect giving him charity. When you say, "We remember what you have done and will do what we can on your behalf," the principle is entirely different.
As has been pointed out, many veterans do not ask for help at the time an injury occurs to them. As a result 20 or 30 years later they find they have been damaged as a result of their war activities, but have no proof that the damage resulted from war service. This is very important, particularly if, as I think is

We all know that there is very little benefit of the doubt given to our veterans. Those of us who have had to deal with veterans' problems know that a man must have almost incontestable proof his injury resulted from war service before he is eligible for assistance. The motion before us is one way of assisting the veteran in this regard, and it would be a more dignified way than we have adopted in the past. However, by accepting the principle of the motion we open the door to other things. Perhaps the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) will excuse me if I add some of my own ideas to the motion and say that we should go beyond what he requests. I am certain of that, although it might be five or eight years from now. Let us get rid of this benefit of doubt situation. Let us go beyond the prisoners of war, although I agree that the principle of starting there is a good and valid one. Let us recognize the great work that the sons and daughters of Canada did on behalf of their country and be generous, humane and grateful for their efforts.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF FORMER PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this notice of motion deals with a more limited number of men than might be seen at first blush. The purpose of it is to bring within medical survey those members of Canada's active armed forces during world war II who were prisoners of war and who have not, for one reason or another, been medically examined in the last five years by either the Canadian Pension Commission or someone on its behalf or by the treatment services of the Department of Veterans Affairs. The purpose of this motion is not to establish pensions for prisoners of war, but rather to do for some of them what was so needed for the Hong Kong prisoners of war. I will be the first one to admit that the degree of privation and malnutrition of European prisoners of war, except perhaps in the odd case, was not nearly as severe as it was in the case of the Hong Kong prisoners of war. It


took a lot of pushing and prodding by members of the opposition and by some members on the government side some three or four years ago to have all of those members of the Hong Kong force who could be located examined.
There is a rather ironic incident that was told to me by a member of that force who comes from Saskatchewan. I met him during the last election campaign. He said he was called in for an examination and he went to Regina to be examined to see whether he had suffered any disability as a result of having been in Japanese hands. Whom did he meet but a Japanese doctor who was acting on behalf of the Pension Commission. Sometimes some people just do not use their heads. It put both men in a very difficult position. I am sure that the doctor himself would not have willingly accepted that task if he had known what was going to happen. What this Hong Kong veteran said to me afterwards was not printable and certainly should not be repeated. He did not think much of the type of service that had been given to him.
The Dieppe Prisoner of War Association was organized by a former Royal Canadian Engineer, one of the real sluggers. This chap by the name of Sandy Shusterman is now a taxi driver in Toronto, and an indefatigable man working in the interest of prisoners of war. The Dieppe Prisoner of War Association has tried to encourage prisoners of war to get together to make representations. They should emulate New Zealand Veterans. I have never seen such a strong organization of veterans as the New Zealand Prisoner of War Association who have been very active in keeping the interests of their members before the governing authorities.
The purpose of this motion-and both the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Macintosh) and I collaborated very closely on this-is to get those men who have not been seen by the Pension Commission or the treatment services within the last years, examined and documented. For one thing preventive medicine is better than curative medicine at any time and, as my colleague said, the records of illnesses during those two or three years that the men were imprisoned were not very complete.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there have been occasions when I have had to make a personal statement in support of one of those people who were in my camp attesting to the fact that this man had suffered from a cold and from certain privations because 10 or 15
February 3, 1969

Canada Evidence Act
years after liberation he developed tuberculosis or some other ailment of which there was no record. Because the man happened to have an old bronchial scar which showed up in his discharge records, it was said that the scar had been incurred prior to service. Every kind of excuse was given to refuse a legitimate claim to benefits while the man was undergoing treatment to cure tuberculosis. There were other ailments, such as stomach illnesses. I know of several men who are suffering from arthritis and nerves. There were also cases of alcoholism. Unfortunately, I know of several chaps in the same camp as I was who have undergone serious bouts of nervous depression. For some of them it has been too much, and they have done away with themselves.
If I had continued as minister, it would have been my aim to bring all of those men in and have them examined long before now. Such an examination would give us the records of what privation and malnutrition will do. I also suggest to the members of this house that in the long run it would save us some money because some of these men are going to develop serious illnesses which may be attributable to pensionable disabilities. Their lives will be shortened. We may be faced with heavy expense in treating a disease or some disability that is pensionable, and there may be a great argument about it. They become very hard cases. We should catch these conditions early and deal with them. Not only are we salvaging a veteran and adding some years to his life, but we will be learning more about the effects of the type of life veterans had to endure for some period of time. As I said, there are not that many men. Among the Dieppe prisoners, there were over 2,000. A number of them, like myself, have been through the hands of the Pension Commission for one reason or another. Some of them are now dead. On the army side there are not that many who have not been checked out. I would say today that the men we are really looking for are chaps from the air force because over the period from September 1939 to May 1945 many of the prisoners of war were airmen who had been shot down. The certainly outnumber the army prisoners of war.
I do not say that a prisoner of war has a greater claim to consideration from the point of view of sentiment or of the duty that he performed. He was a serviceman like many others, but he did not have to go through battle, as many did. So far as I was concerned, I was in one battle and that was it.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
I do not say my treatment was worse than that of many other servicemen. We did tend to lose an awful lot of weight, and I did not weigh nearly as much when I was captured as I do now. But all my friends in my old regiment say the same thing, there is something in each case which goes back to those days when we were incarcerated in cold buildings during the winter and given poor food to eat. Then, there were the mental pressures, and so on. So, I make a plea to the government to take up this question. There are not many men involved, relatively, and I do not believe the expense would be great. It would take some time to organize, but I think something should be done. I will put the question-
