AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen (for the Minister of Justice) for the third reading of Bill S-3, to amend the Canada Evidence Act.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make prior to consideration of the actual contents of Bill S-3. The first matter I want to raise may result from inadvertence, and I want to give the government house leader every break that is possible. Both of us are members of the committee on procedure and realize that the purpose of the change in the rules governing the legislative process was to shift the emphasis in the debate to the report stage and the third reading. Over the dinner hour, I searched diligently but could find no record of the transcript of our discussions in the

February 3, 1969
Canada Evidence Act
justice committee relating to this bill. How on earth can any reasonable person expect the members of this house to be able to discuss this or any other bill under these circumstances, having changed our procedure to put greater emphasis on the value of committee hearings?
As has been said by members on both sides of the house, hon. members of the house were to be given the opportunity to delve into the details of the bill and put their comments on record at committee hearings. In this way, they would not waste the time of the house asking questions. There are some sections of this bill that bother me.
I also went through the records of the Senate, with no cumulative index to assist me, to see when the legislation was handled there. What one has to do, Mr. Speaker, is to take the Hansard report of the other place and go through it section by section to see when the bill went through second reading, when it went through committee, and when it was read a third time. Third reading in the Senate occupied four lines. In other words, the record of the other place, as far as I and other hon. members are concerned, revealed precisely nil by way of any explanation of this bill, and was of no assistance.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Abolish it.

I would not agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) there, because I have gone back to the reports of a committee of the other place that has examined the bill with care and the evidence and questioning have been of great help. But in this particular case, I cannot rely on what happened in the other place.
I hope that the government house leader, in calling this bill, was not aware that our own reports were not ready. In such circumstances, how are we going to place proper emphasis on the report stage and on third reading? We have downgraded second reading stage by having fewer speakers and by-agreeing that bills go to committee for examination so that hon. members are equipped to deal with them there. Yet, here we have this particular item called in the house and we have nothing to assist us. Either we have to stop this nonsense here and now, or what we hoped and I think quite rightly, was to be a change for the better in our procedure will go for naught.
[Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West).}
It must be remembered that there are certain housekeeping requirements between hearing evidence in committees and the appearance of the reports which are made available to hon. members. I may be wrong about this; I thought my search during the dinner hour was a rather thorough one. I know that my secretary is a fairly faithful and competent woman who keeps my filings up to date. But as I say, I looked and looked and I could find no reports. If hon. members correct me and tell me that the reports regarding the study of Bill S-3 are in their hands, then I will apologize. Until that is established I will say that the calling of this bill at this time was an imposition on the house. It was quite unfair. I hope we are not left in the position, with other bills to come before us, of not having in our possession copies of the committee hearings. I know certain committees work faster than others, and I have no cause for complaint about the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, of which I am a member. Everything works fairly well in that committee; bills are sent to us to be studied and transcripts of proceedings are readily forthcoming.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I wish to emphasize that unless steps can be taken t o schedule properly the report stages and third reading stages of bills before this house, we ought to forget the new rules and revert back to the old rules. We ought to have committee transcripts in our hands at report and third reading stages.
Hear, hear.

I am not
saying the old rules necessarily were any better than our present rules; but please do not say you are going to make a change, claim advantages for that change, and then not deliver the goods.
They cannot deliver the evidence given before the committee.

My next point is made with all due apology and is not meant personally against any parliamentary secretary. I support my colleague for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and other hon. members of the house-after all, we have reached a stage of particular importance with regard to this bill-who asked for the responsible minister to be here to answer to the house. The parliamentary secretary may be able to give us certain information, but under our
February 3, 1969

system parliamentary secretaries have no responsibility. For this house to question the parliamentary secretary and hold him responsible for answers touching questions of policy is quite improper under the rules unless the roles of parliamentary secretaries are changed. Personally, I should like parliamentary secretaries to be given greater responsibilities. Their positions ought to have some tangible meaning. But that has not been done. All power is kept in tight, grubby little hands.
Grubby or crummy.

It is only
natural for members like the hon. member for Calgary North to be concerned about the implications of clause 2 of the bill, which amends section 9 of the Canada Evidence Act. If ever a clause sought to load the dice in favour of the prosecution, it is clause 2. I see the parliamentary secretary shaking his head. I hope he has had even one tenth the experience in court of the hon. member for Calgary North, to say nothing of the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). This clause purports to say that when a witness is to be declared hostile a statement merely has to be made to the court to the effect that there is a difference between the evidence being given at the moment and evidence that was given elsewhere. The prior evidence must be reduced to writing. The court then is invited to declare the witness hostile. I say that is wrong. There must be proof of the facts alleged. A witness ought not to be declared hostile merely on the word of one man. After all, the entire matter ought to be looked into by way of examination and cross examination.
The hon. parliamentary secretary may not have the experience that trial lawyers have had with preliminary hearings, apres enquete. It is not necessary for defence counsel to call witnesses. Defence counsel has the right to examine the Crown's witnesses to see what kind of case the Crown has. There is a stage in justice where a preliminary hearing is held in order for the court to determine if there is sufficient evidence to substantiate the charge. That is, if there is a prima facie case. The accused or his counsel have the inalienable right to examine every iota of evidence put forward by the Crown to determine whether there is evidence to substantiate the laying of the charge. Of course, the Crown calls its witnesses, not necessarily all of them, to substantiate the validity of the charge, in the judgment of the Crown. That evidence is
Canada Evidence Act
recorded. Later, if there is the slightest difference between the evidence given at the preliminary inquiry and the evidence given at trial, the Crown prosecutor does not even have to prove the preliminary hearing transcript, because the wording of clause 2(2) is:
Where the party producing a witness alleges that the witness made at other times a statement in writing, or reduced to writing, inconsistent with his present testimony, the court may, without proof that the witness is adverse-
And so on and so forth. That is how a witness may be declared adverse and to my way of thinking this clause attempts to load the dice in favour of the Crown.
The minister ought to be here, Mr. Speaker. What were the government's reasons for bringing in such amendments? It must have had its reasons, although we do not know them not being possessed of the testimony given before the committee. We do not know what that testimony was and yet we are asked to pass this bill. The basic reason the hon. member who sought to adjourn debate on this bill this afternoon had for bringing forward his motion was that there is no transscript before the house of the evidence taken in committee. We therefore wonder why the government has advanced these amendments to this section.
I find myself very embarrassed, Mr. Speaker, at third reading to be asking such questions. After all, I am not a member of the committee that studied the bill, and that is the difficulty. Reasons for advancing these amendments may have been furnished before that committee but we do not know of those reasons because we have no transcript. The burden is on the government proposing the change to substantiate the need for this change in the law. The clause appears to me, and I am a lawyer, to be loading the dice in favour of the prosecution. That is all I will say on the point. But before I consent to passage of this bill, there must be a satisfactory explanation of the government's thinking. That explanation might be made available either through adjourning the debate so that we can obtain the transcript of evidence taken before the committee or by calling the minister-or at least having him present in the house-and allowing him to explain the government's thinking on the matter.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
My second point deals with clause 3 which purports to amend section 29 of the act and the definition of a financial institution. Again I wish we had the transcript of the committee

February 3, 1969
Canada Evidence Act
proceedings. Does a financial institution as defined under section 29(3)-I am referring to the bottom of page 3 of the bill-include treasury branches in the province of Alberta? There is a recent case, Green versus the Treasury Branch of Alberta and other parties, which alleges as a defence that the Treasury Branch is not a financial institution within the meaning of the act. This case went to the Supreme Court of Canada. Bill S-3, at the top of page 4 reads in part:
-any institution incorporated in Canada-
It is my information the Treasury Branches of the Province of Alberta are merely emanations of the treasury of the provincial government. I have never known the treasury of a province to be deemed to be incorporated. Therefore, by omission, do we perhaps have here a form of financial institution? These branches do a tremendous business in the Province of Alberta. One can consider the volume of business being transacted by the Caisse Populaire in the Province of Quebec which is comparable to the Treasury Branches in Alberta.

What did you say?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member if he is aware that the amendment has been requested by the credit unions of the province of Alberta?

caisses populaires of the province of Quebec.

speechtext: By the credit unions.

Very well, but I am referring to the Treasury Branches-

Treasury branches are financial institutions carrying on the business of banking, and yet they have not been incorporated. Undoubtedly there was legislation in the past authorizing the government of the Province of Alberta to create branches of the provincial treasury. I would like to know from the minister-
He isn't here.

-or perhaps then the parliamentary secretary, as to whether the question of the provincial treasury branches of the Province of Alberta has

been considered in the light of this amendment. If not, then somebody had better do their homework. The debate should be adjourned and the necessary amendment moved to cover the point.
I have approached this bill as a Member of Parliament as well as a member of the legal profession. I have been unable to obtain any information regarding this act. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I have belaboured the point but I want to emphasize it and over-emphasize it, not only for this act but for other acts. My point is that unless and until the committee system is working sufficiently well to have the transcript of evidence before the members of this house no bill can be considered. I stress this point to the government house leader, and ask him to clarify this point. I am certain the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome), who is a lawyer as well as a member of the Procedure Committee will agree with me on this point. On that point, I would like to hear from both the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and the government house leader.

I do not
intend to speak very long on this bill. I am a member of the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee and I share the feelings of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) when he complained of the absence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). I also agree with his complaint that we are asked to deal with the bill at this stage without having available to us the transcript of evidence given before the committee.
Having said that, I would now like to say that I see nothing difficult, sinister or improper regarding that section of the bill. It is a perfectly reasonable section and speaks for itself. It states, "the court may" not that "the prosecution may".
Without proof.
Without proof, certainly. Without proof of what? Without proof that the witness is adverse, a procedure which every practising lawyer realizes is a stupid procedure,-
Hear, hear.

-whereby a witness must be provoked into some exhibition of irritation before being declared adverse. If this is not
February 3, 1969

done the witness cannot be cross-examined although he has been tampered with, has given a written statement, and is now giving a totally inconsistent statement. This amendment makes more sense than the law as it now is, and I do not know why so much time is being wasted on it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I rise to deal with some of the observations made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I can assure him that his researches are correct. I am advised that the transcript of evidence is not now available of the proceedings in that committee. I am also advised that the committee on Tuesday, January 28 dealt with the bill for approximately one hour. No amendments were moved to change any provisions of this bill and more particularly with regard to the section which has so much concerned the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and the hon. member for Edmonton West. I can assure them there was no attempt to take advantage of hon. members. The assumption was made, because of the apparent non-controversial aspect of the bill, that we could proceed.
When I stated to the house on Friday that it would be called as the third item of business for today I understood there would be no objection to proceeding with it because there appeared to be general agreement with the terms of the bill. I do not think I have to apologize to the hon. member for Calgary North because he is a member of the committee and knows his rights. He could have exercised them in the Committee.
This bill has been before parliament for many months. It started, Mr. Speaker, in the other place. It was on the record of, and considered by, the other place for some time. It was then referred to this house. It was not a bill which was hidden behind a money resolution. These terms have been available to the house for a very long time, and to the hon. member in particular. The bill was referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, where it was considered and dealt with quite expeditiously. I think we had reason to believe there was no particular contest with respect to its terms. It was because of the understanding there was no contest that it was called forward to be dealt with by the house.

It is never good to make assumptions.
Canada Evidence Act

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I realize it is never good to make assumptions about the hon. members opposite. I must say I am concerned about the latent interest in this bill, but I think it can be reasonably said there was plenty of opportunity for investigation. No amendments were put forward at the committee stage. No hon. members, such as the hon. member for Calgary North, put forward any amendments. My understanding was that the evidence would be available, but as I understand it there are different timetables for preparing the evidence and I quite appreciate the reasons for that.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
On the whole I feel that no injustice has been done by calling the bill at this time. It seems to me that if any hon. member felt hard done by, then I might have heard about it before the middle of this afternoon and been told that members felt the bill should not be brought forward.
The only other comment of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) that I wish to deal with is his objection to the fact that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cantin) has charge of the conduct of this bill. I might recall to hon. members the fact that my colleague, the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, has had the conduct of a great many pieces of legislation in this house, for which the hon. member for Edmonton West had the responsibility of speaking for this party on that side of the house.
With respect to the complaint of the hon. member for Edmonton West that the parliamentary secretary has the conduct of this bill-and I might read into his reference "a mere parliamentary secretary," and I say this as one who for five years was a parliamentary secretary-I say that the parliamentary secretary is fully capable of taking the bill through all its stages in this house, in committee, and everywhere.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I therefore say, Mr. Speaker, that there is no precedent for a valid objection to the conduct of legislation through this house by one of my colleagues who is a parliamentary secretary, and in particular by my colleague, the parliamentary

February 3, 1969
Canada Evidence Act
secretary from Quebec. I say there is no authority for that proposition whatsoever, and it is entirely within the proprieties when a qualified colleague of mine, such as the parliamentary secretary from Quebec, has the conduct of this particular bill.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that I am not in a position to debate the merits of the bill. This has not been my responsibility. But I notice that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), who has had a great deal of trial experience, who was a member of the standing committee and who participated in its deliberations, takes a different legal point of view from that of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). Again, I assert that there was no surprise and no unfairness in the calling of this bill at this time. If there was a feeling of surprise, if hon. members really after a period of months were not prepared to go ahead with the bill, then I submit that I should have been told about it prior to the calling of the bill this afternoon. On the whole, it seems to me it would be reasonable to go ahead and give the bill third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I rise somewhat hesitantly to speak on a bill dealing mainly with matters which might well concern members of the legal profession. I admit quite openly that I am not a member of the legal profession but I have always believed that justice must be fair, must be just, and also must appear to be just and fair. On reading over clause 2 at the top of page 4 of this bill, I can hardly assume that the measure appears to be fair.
I have listened to the arrogant member for Rosedale-
Oh, oh.

-the hon. member for Rose-dale (Mr. Macdonald), if hon. members prefer that, tell us that nobody suggested there was any opposition to the bill and therefore we had better rush it through parliament in a hurry. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I ask hon. members opposite what would have happened if we had rushed through the estate taxes bill in a hurry, on October 22 last? What would have been the effect on the public today?
Hear, hear.

That was not done. In the interim, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) heard an outcry and some changes have been made in that bill. I do not believe enough Changes were made, but this was one good

effect from having some feedback, some delay, some criticism and some thinking about the bill.
I was not a member of the standing committee that examined this bill, but I was a member of the rules committee.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Until you were replaced.

Until I was replaced, as the hon. member for Rosedale says. I had an opportunity to travel overseas on a NATO committee at a time when I thought the government was reversing its stand on NATO, and I thought I should concern myself more with that problem.
Like the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans).

I reluctantly gave up my position on the rules committee but before doing so I firmly understood that no bills, after examination in committee, would be debated on third reading until the committee proceedings had been printed and all hon. members of the house had an opportunity to examine them.
A parliamentary secretary on the government benches may well say, "Well, there was no opposition. We had no trouble about this." I reply that all 264 members of the House of Commons are of equal importance. My constituency, the constituency of Crowfoot, is of equal importance to that of any other constituency in the country. Therefore, I should be given the opportunity, the right to examine the evidence to ascertain whether or not this bill purports to be fair, purports to be just, and in my mind and in my constituents' minds contributes to the just society in which I and my constituents might well believe.
From my brief skimming through the bill, and in particular through clause 2, and without having the committee evidence before me, I cannot honestly say that a witness should be re-examined without proof in any way, shape or form that he is an adverse witness.
Again, with respect to the clause dealing with banking institutions I do not believe it should exclude provincial treasury branches. When the question of banking institutions came up in the debate on the bill amending the Farm Credit Corporations Act I spoke of the part the treasury branches played in the province of Alberta in creating competition. We in this party believe competition is the guide to efficiency, is the key to efficiency in this society of ours which is founded on free
February 3, 1969

Canada Evidence Act
enterprise. But hon. members to the right of you, Mr. Speaker, believe that if they can hide the evidence-and this is the only conclusion I can draw-then ignorance is bliss; all shall pass and everybody will forgive because in the name of the just society everything is right and nothing is wrong.
I don't believe that because I believe that justice must appear to be just. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) says, in effect, that in the past the way in which this matter has been handled in the courts has been ridiculous and therefore we might as well pass this amending legislation. A number of members in the Hitler administration, Ger-hardt included, believed, "We must push on; we must reach decisions in a hurry." The suggestion is that counsel must be given the right to cross-examine their own witnesses if they find the witnesses are adverse, but without proof that they are adverse. I cannot for the life of me understand why they do not know that beforehand. They call them as witnesses in the first instance.
The minister who has just spoken was the chairman of the rules committee. He reported to the house on the rules. He cannot honestly say-

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, and just as a matter of accuracy the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) was the chairman of the rules committee.
I accept the point of privilege. The minister wasn't the chairman of the rules committee.
The Gray Eminence.
He was the gray eminence of the chairman of the rules committee. He dominated the rules committee-
As Mr. Goebbels.

He brought the wishes of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) into the rules committee. One of the clear, explicit understandings of the rules committee was that after second reading a bill should be passed to a committee. Then the committee would examine it extensively, and after extensive examination the bill should come back into the house for third reading. At that time the committee evidence would be printed and each member of the house would have the evidence of the committee available to him.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
This has not been done in respect of this bill, and I issue a warning to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to every member opposite in the government that this should not happen again with regard to other committee proceedings. This is not fair or just. It is no more fair or just than this bill appears to be when it refers to witnesses being declared hostile without proof. Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on third reading of Bill C-152 I am glad to report that this was one time when there was general agreement amongst all party members on both sides of the house in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. The Committee only had to clarify and verify items in the bill concerning the welfare of a very important segment of our population, thus giving recognition to those who make up a very important part of our nation, the war veterans. This bill exemplifies the realization of all members of parliament that it is the duty of the government of Canada to continually review and provide for the war veterans, so that they can have the opportunity of providing a livelihood for themselves and their families.
It is significant that today, in this House of Commons, a notice of motion was put forth by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) asking the government to give consideration to the immediate organization of a program of medical examination of all members of the Canadian active service forces who were prisoners of war in world war II and who have not been examined in the past five years. This shows that we, as representatives of the citizens of this country, must constantly be reminded of the part played by war veterans in the building of this great nation of Canada. This is a responsibility that we must never take lightly.
We, as members of the committee, were pleased that the rate of interest on loans up to $6,000, which was established in 1942 at 3) per cent, will not be affected by this bill. The main item of change will permit the rate on loans of over $6,000 and up to $20,000 to be determined from time to time by the Governor in Council. In this regard I feel it should be mentioned that the Royal Canadian Legion, who represent the majority of war veterans in Canada, recognized the sharp increase in recent years in mortgage rates, bond interest and the rate of interest on money lent by the Bank of Canada. They, therefore, recommended that the rate be that

paid by the government to secure the necessary funds, with administrative costs being borne by the government.
I wholeheartedly agree with the recommendation of the Royal Canadian Legion; but we are all prepared to realize as responsible citizens-and I am sure the war veteran realizes too-that as the cost of money increases progressively this extra cost must be borne by all citizens who need to borrow.
I, and the members of the standing committee from the opposition side, are satisfied that the veteran who applies for the average loan of, say, $20,000 will be in the slightly preferred category that he deserves. On a loan of this proportion he will pay an average of a little over 6 per cent, because he will be paying 3 J per cent on the first $6,000 and 7| per cent on the remainder.
We are concerned, however, about the availability of funds. We are concerned that the amount available each year has dropped until it is now $74 million. We hope that we will not hear the old cries of "restraint in spending" and "feasibility studies" and "task forces" coming to the fore. We hope money will be provided for loans to veterans for as long as they are required, and that the amount provided will be commensurate with the needs of all applicants. I am prepared, however, to believe that the government is aware of the debt we owe the veterans of this country and will live up to its responsibility to make available the necessary funds which will continue to provide opportunities for these important citizens of Canada.

He said: It gives me great pleasure, Mr. Speaker to recommend the two basic amendments in this bill for approval by this house.
I may say in explanation of the main overseas telecommunications service that it was formed in 1949. It was established for a number of purposes among which the most important was to establish, maintain and operate in Canada and elsewhere external communications services for the conduct of public communications.
Since 1949 until the present time, Mr. Speaker, this Crown Corporation has had an enviable history of accomplishment and achievement. It has accomplished very well all of the objectives which the government and the people of Canada laid down for it in 1949.
At the present time it is a corporation with assets exceeding $83 million. Its revenue last year was $24 million and it showed a profit of $4 million. The corporation has shown a profit for every one of the 18 years it has been in existence and during that time has paid to the government over $20 million in interest charges, $19,912,000 in income tax, and has returned $16 million of its advances from the government. The officers and employees of the corporation have proved themselves capable of managing their affairs in the interests of the Canadian people and I think that is a real justification.
Their past record justifies their request at this time, which I am happy to put forward, for additional powers and greater flexibility. The corporation is a member of the International Telecommunication Satellite Consortium and represents Canada on that board. It is much concerned with the expansion of satellite services all over the world and of course maintains Canada's interest and attention in all that goes on in international satellite relations. The corporation itself is expanding the use of Atlantic satellites to cope with the
[Mr. Speaker.)

need for more capacity to cater for increasing demand for service between Canada and European countries and foresees the need for a Canadian earth station on the West coast for operations with the Pacific satellites. As is well known the corporation some years ago built an earth station at Mill Village in Nova Scotia at a cost of some $12 million. An additional earth station is now being built there which will have the capacity to receive communications from satellites including the French satellite when it is launched.
I feel the people in Canada should be more aware of the contribution that this corporation makes. At the present time it has inaugurated overseas dataphone service and it expects this service also will be very profitable. This has been background information for the benefit of hon. members and I will now go to the bill specifically, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
As it noted in Bill S-5, we wish to amend section 2(f). In the original act section 2(f) says:
"external telecommunication services" means the telecommunication services between Canada and any place outside of Canada and between Newfoundland and any other part of Canada;
Section 6(b) also makes reference to "Newfoundland and any other part of Canada." When the corporation was formed Newfoundland had become Canada's tenth province but from a telecommunications point of view it was overseas and the service was provided by the Canadian Marconi Company by high frequency radio.
When under the act, chapter 42 (1949) the C.O.T.C. was formed, the corporation expropriated the property and equipment of the Canadian Marconi Company used in connection with its external services; that is, radio stations at Drummondville and Yamachiche. It was not practical at that time to exclude from the total expropriation that part of the equipment used for service with Newfoundland, although it had by that time become the tenth province.
The corporation undertook to provide the additional facilities necessary to meet the growing demand for service between the island and the mainland. However, it rapidly became clear that this service should more properly rest in the hands of a domestic carrier and accordingly after lengthy negotiations these facilities were transferred to Canadian National Telecommunications on January 1, 1966. Therefore, to bring this act
February 3, 1969

up to date it is desirable to remove the references to Newfoundland.
With respect to the second amendment that We recommend, the figures that I have quoted give you some idea of the tremendous performance, the strength and the size of the corporation, and therefore of the capacity of the people who direct it to handle their own affairs. Their power, flexibility and ability to make decisions are gravely limited by a section in the original act which reads:
Unless the approval of the Governor in Council is first obtained, the corporation shall not
(a) enter into an agreement involving any expenditure in excess of fifty thousand dollars:
With the establishment of cable systems between Bermuda, Canada and other countries, and with the corporation investing in satellite systems and switching systems, it is continually coming before Treasury Board for approval of a number of decisions that we feel the directors should have the power to make themselves. For example, during the last six years Orders in Council were requested for 146 different actions taken by the board of directors. I seriously question whether any more than 30 or 40 of those should have been forthcoming. That was one part of the limitation of power. Subparagraph (b) was another and provides that the corporation shall not:
-enter into for a period exceeding three years any agreement or lease that involves an expenditure in any year of more than five thousand dollars;
Hon. members will realize that when a corporation with annual revenues of $24 million, with assets exceeding $80 million, with total fixed assets in the order of $97 million-that, of course, is not the depreciated figure-is faced with a limitation on the directors that they shall not enter into any lease involving an expenditure of more than $5,000 in any year, it is a serious limitation.
Then there is another limitation in subparagraph (c) which says that the corporation shall not:
-acquire any real or personal property, the cost of acquisition of which exceeds the sum of fifty thousand dollars, or in any manner dispose of any such property having an original or book value exceeding the sum of five thousand dollars.
Just two or three weeks ago I had to approve a request to the Treasury Board that the corporation be permitted to sell some used, obsolete equipment the original value of 29180-322*
Business of the House
which was about $9,000. These amendments will avoid this procedure. It is time consuming. It limits the capacity of the directors to handle their own affairs, a capacity which has been well demonstrated during the years, and so I heartily recommend that these amendments be approved.

the minister a question before he sits down, Mr. Speaker. Would he explain how the administration of the corporation gets greater powers under the amendment in clause 3 of the bill than it had before, when it needs to have the recommendation of the Treasury Board and the approval of the Governor in Council before it enters into any agreement or lease?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, LIMITATION OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: What will happen is that the Treasury Board will lay down the same rules that apply to other crown corporations. The Treasury Board will prescribe such limits as it may consider to be appropriate. In other words, the limitations presently listed in the legislation may not be the limitations which the Treasury Board will set. The corporation has to be under some control but that control would be less, at least as to physical amount, than presently exists.

The hon. member for Nickel Belt.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, last week I directed to the secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) a question concerning some recommendations of the Franco-Ontari-an Committee on cultural life which were presented to the Ontario Minister of Education.
That report contains some very important recommendations on federal institutions which come under the central government.
In my question, I asked the Secretary of State whether he intended to answer favourably the request of the Franco-Ontarian Committee on cultural life that the C.B.C. establish French radio stations (AM and FM) and television stations wherever there is a sufficient number of French-speaking people in Ontario.
As I have been unable to get from the Secretary of State an answer to that question which is, I feel, of capital importance, not only to French-speaking people in Ontario but also to English-speaking people and to the whole country, I was bent on raising it tonight.
In order that the Secretary of State, hon. members and the Canadian people might have a better understanding of the purport of my question, I hasten to quote two recommendations made by the Franco-Ontarian Committee on cultural life. The first one reads as follows:
That French radio and television stations, in Ontario continue to be supplied through Montreal, but that local and regional production centres be established in Ottawa, Toronto, Windsor and Sudbury so as to form a Franco-Ontarian radio and television network.

The system, while complying with the standards of quality approved by the C.B.C., would be responsible for Ontario public affairs and the development of local talent.
The second recommendation reads as follows:
That the C.B.C., while maintaining its standards of quality, offer programming which is better suited to the interests of Franco-Ontarians, when the C.B.C. station is the only French-speaking one in an area.
Mr. Speaker, the C.B.C. has certainly made great efforts to help the Franco-Ontarians in the last few years, but the present services are far from satisfactory.
It is worth noting that in Ontario, there is only one French television station, CBOFT, the C.B.C. station in Ottawa, and that there is no other private French television station.
The Corporation offers French television to a great number of French Canadians of the "Middle North" of Ontario, that is the Sudbury and North Bay region, and to those of the "Far North" or the Timmins, Kapuskasing and Hearst area. Of course, this is a great help to the French Canadians of Northern Ontario, but it is not enough, because often they do not have much interest in programs originating in Montreal and Quebec City. Besides, and that is the most important point, for the French-Canadians of Southern Ontario who are quite numerous, there is no French television station at all.
Mr. Speaker, if we accept the principles underlayng the Canadian constitution, if we recognize the bilingual and bicultural nature of Canada, if we sincerely want to safeguard the French-Canadian culture in North America, we must think of taking immediate steps to correct the gross injustice being done to almost three-quarters of a million Franco-Ontarians and to provide them quickly with the means not only to survive but also to develop in a normal way.
We all agree that mass media can play a leading role as a medium of culture. However, without any newspapers, radio or TV of their own, Franco-Ontarians are bound to disappear, as is now the case, considering the increasing number of them who are unavoidably assimilated.
Mr. Speaker, the Franco-Ontarians are not asking for any privileges, they are only demanding their rights. They are only asking for the same treatment the English-speaking minority gets in Quebec. In every Quebec community where there is a sufficient number of English-speaking people, the latter can
February 3, 1969

enjoy radio and television in their own language.
We must stop identifying French Canada with Quebec and recognize that French Canada comprises Ontario, New Brunswick and reaches out to the west, across the whole continent. The government, under the clever leadership of our present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) undertook to protect the rights of minorities; it undertook to promote bilingualism and biculturalism across the country wherever it is deemed necessary and the people of Canada have accepted that fact, judging from the results of the June 25 election. I know the Secretary of State is more than inclined to do something in this respect.
If Ontario becomes a truly bilingual province where the two great cultures will be allowed to develop and enlarge through one another, in the most complete harmony, it will become an example of good understanding and of co-operation for the other provinces. This will belie the views held by some Quebec extremists by proving to them that Confederation can and will operate and thus we will have taken a great step toward the achievement of national unity.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask once again the Secretary of State if he intends to assent to the recommendations of the Franco-Ontarian Committee on cultural life.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that the recommendations of the Franco-Ontarian Committee on cultural life have been considered with

As a matter of fact, the C.B.C. has established an internal committee to consider the whole matter of broadcasting in French. This matter is now being considered by the officials of the corporation and it is hoped that a policy might be implemented as funds become available.
I call the hon. member's attention to the fact that a new French language radio station has been licensed in Windsor, Ontario, and that the possibility of issuing a permit for the operation of a television station is now under study.

I might also mention that the C.B.C. is hoping to make application in the near future for French television service in my own city, the third largest French speaking city in Canada, Toronto, and also Pembroke. Another area the C.B.C. is seriously considering for this service at the present time is the whole northern Ontario region in which my hon. friend is so interested. Extension of service is planned for that region in accordance with the representations of the hon. member and his colleagues from northern Ontario. I am advised, too, that other communities are also in the corporation's mind. The whole question of French language service is of great, current concern to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
